Close, but flip it back, friend. The father says, “Keep my commandments and live…” (Proverbs 7:2). The word "live" is sitting right there in the verse. So his commandments point toward life. It's an easy one to flip when you read fast, and I've done it with a timer or two.

explanations.answer: On his fingers and his heart
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. The father says, “Tie them to your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.” (Proverbs 7:3). One is right out front where his hands can see it, and the other goes deep inside. It's like a string tied on your finger so you don't forget, except this one gets written on the heart too.

explanations.answer: On his doorposts and his gates
explanations.explanation: That one does ring a bell. Moses, Israel's leader, told Israel to write God's words on the doorposts of their houses and on their gates (Deuteronomy 6:9). But this father says something different in Proverbs. He says, “Tie them to your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.” (Proverbs 7:3). So the places here are the fingers and the heart.

explanations.answer: On a scroll and a stone tablet
explanations.explanation: You're close, because the word "tablet" really is in the verse. But look at what kind of tablet it is. The father says, “Tie them to your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.” (Proverbs 7:3). So it's a tablet of the heart, not stone, and there's no scroll in the verse at all. A little to the left of the right answer, friend.

Yes, friend. The father sees “…a young man lacking judgment…” (Proverbs 7:7). He says it right as he's picking him out from among the simple and the youths. I think he's saying the young man's problem isn't speed or strength. It's that his good sense isn't switched on.

I get it, friend. Courage is what you'd expect somebody to be missing. But the verse says something else. The father notices “…a young man lacking judgment…” (Proverbs 7:7). So the word is judgment, not courage.
Nice try, friend, though nobody's checking his wallet here. The father notices “…a young man lacking judgment…” (Proverbs 7:7). The verse says nothing about money. What he's short on is good sense.

explanations.answer: At twilight as day fades to dark
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The verse says it's “…at twilight, as the day was fading into the dark of the night.” (Proverbs 7:9). The light is going out while he walks. I think the father wants us to notice how dim it's getting on this road.

explanations.answer: At sunrise as the city wakes up
explanations.explanation: Sunrise is the opposite end of the day, friend. The verse puts the young man on the road “…at twilight, as the day was fading into the dark of the night.” (Proverbs 7:9). So the light is going away, not coming up. This one happens at the end of the day, not the start.

explanations.answer: At noon in the heat of the day
explanations.explanation: Noon would have the sun straight overhead, friend. The father says it's “…at twilight, as the day was fading into the dark of the night.” (Proverbs 7:9). That's evening, with the light draining out of the sky. No midday heat in this scene.

That's right, friend. The father says, “She is loud and defiant; her feet do not remain at home.” (Proverbs 7:11). So she's loud and defiant, and home isn't where she stays. It's the opposite of quiet and settled.

Look at the verse again, friend. She says, “…I came out to meet you; I sought you, and I have found you.” (Proverbs 7:15). Those are her own words to him. So she does say she sought him and found him.

Not this time, friend. She tells him, “For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey.” (Proverbs 7:19). So what she says is that he's away, not at home. That's her pitch to the young man.

You've got it, friend. She says, “For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey.” (Proverbs 7:19). She's telling the young man her husband is away. Next verse she says how long he'll be gone.

explanations.answer: Not till the moon is full
explanations.explanation: Exactly, friend. She says her husband “…took with him a bag of money and will not return till the moon is full.” (Proverbs 7:20). That's the timing she gives. She also says he's on a long journey (Proverbs 7:19), and she's telling this to the young man at twilight (Proverbs 7:9).

That's not the timing she gives, friend. She says her husband “…took with him a bag of money and will not return till the moon is full.” (Proverbs 7:20). So she's talking about a full moon, not a sunrise. She makes it sound like a long wait.

explanations.answer: At the end of the week
explanations.explanation: That's not the timing she gives, friend. She says her husband “…took with him a bag of money and will not return till the moon is full.” (Proverbs 7:20). She names the full moon, not a day of the week. The bag of money is in there too, so the trip sounds big.

Gifts would make sense in a lot of stories, friend. But the verse says, “With her great persuasion she entices him; with her flattering lips she lures him.” (Proverbs 7:21). Nothing in it says she hands him anything. It's her words that pull him in.

Money does come up in her speech, friend, because she says her husband took a bag of money (Proverbs 7:20). But that's not how the verse says she gets the young man to follow her. explanations.answer: He's being chased by a hunter
explanations.explanation: Look at who's moving, friend. The father says the young man follows her on impulse, “…like a deer bounding into a trap…” (Proverbs 7:22). Nobody is chasing him in the verse. He goes toward the trap without knowing, and the father says it will cost him his life (Proverbs 7:23). It's a sad picture.

explanations.answer: He's strong enough to break free
explanations.explanation: The pictures point the other way, friend. The father uses an ox heading to the slaughter and a deer in a trap, and the young man is “…not knowing it will cost him his life.” (Proverbs 7:23). Nothing in those verses says he breaks free. I think the father is showing how little he sees coming.

explanations.answer: Don't let your heart turn aside to them
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The father says, “Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.” (Proverbs 7:25). He talks about the heart and about the paths in the same breath. I think that's worth hanging onto.

explanations.answer: Talk with her and turn her back
explanations.explanation: The father doesn't give that plan, friend. He says, “Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.” (Proverbs 7:25). There's no stopping to talk in his advice. It's about keeping the heart from turning aside.

explanations.answer: Stay off her paths only at night
explanations.explanation: The father doesn't put a time on it, friend. He says, “Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.” (Proverbs 7:25). It's not an at-night-only rule. He asks his sons to keep their hearts from turning her way at all.
The father says much more than that, friend. He says, “For she has brought many down to death; her slain are many in number.” (Proverbs 7:26). So the number is many, not a few. It's a heavy line.
That's right, friend. The father says, “For she has brought many down to death; her slain are many in number.” (Proverbs 7:26). He says it in two ways, many and many in number. It's a heavy line.

explanations.answer: Down to the chambers of death
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The father says, “Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.” (Proverbs 7:27). Sheol is the place of the dead. The road goes down, not up, which is how he closes the warning.

explanations.answer: Out to a house of feasting
explanations.explanation: It may look inviting at the door, friend, but that's not where the father says it leads. He says, “Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.” (Proverbs 7:27). The passage names the chambers of death as where it descends. It's a sober way to finish.

explanations.answer: Up to the halls of honor
explanations.explanation: The father points the opposite way, friend. He says, “Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.” (Proverbs 7:27). Notice the word descending. It goes down, not up, and honor isn't at the end of it.
